summary: I built a small Node.js (Mongoose) sample app that demonstrates Azure DocumentDB change streams, atomic per-ward summary updates, and TTL expiry for cleaning-state documents. The sample includes an idempotent seed script, a one-shot demo that starts a short-lived change-stream watcher and performs status updates, a small Express API to inspect ward summaries / update bed status, and a README with run instructions. I created indexes (including a TTL index) and verified the app against the live DocumentDB cluster reachable via DOCUMENTDB_URI in the environment. Change-stream processing updated ward summaries as expected. I attempted a quick TTL deletion test (5s expiry) and observed that deletion did not occur within 30s — TTL deletions are driven by a background thread and can be delayed; this is noted in not_verified.
how_to_run: 1) Copy .env.example to .env and set DOCUMENTDB_URI (do NOT commit real secrets). Optionally set CLEANING_TTL_SECONDS and DB_NAME. 2) Install deps: npm install 3) Seed sample data / create indexes: npm run seed 4) Run the demo (starts a short-lived change-stream watcher, performs sample updates, then exits): npm run demo 5) Optional: run the HTTP server to inspect summaries: npm start then GET /wards/ward-A/summary 6) To test TTL behavior manually, adjust CLEANING_TTL_SECONDS in .env and use src/ttl_check.js (npm run demo sets cleaning timestamps; ttl_check tries a short 5s expiry and polls — TTL deletions are subject to background sweep timing).
verification_done: npm install: completed (dependencies installed without vulnerabilities)
npm run check-env: detected DOCUMENTDB_URI in environment (DOCUMENTDB_URI set: true)
npm run seed: ran src/seed.js successfully (output: 'Seeding complete'); seed created collections and indexes and populated sample wards and beds
documentdb_list_databases (via MCP server) for sample_healthcare_12: returned collections 'beds' (count 19) and 'wardsummaries' (count 3)

documentdb_list_indexes (via MCP server) on beds collection: showed indexes including cleaningExpiresAt_1 with expireAfterSeconds: 0 (TTL index present), bedId_1, wardId_1, wardId_1_status_1, status_1

npm run demo: started change-stream watcher, updated several beds and logged updates; change-stream handler recomputed and updated WardSummary documents. Demo output included lines like 'Updated ward summary for ward-A: { occupied: 2, available: 2, cleaning: 2 }'
documentdb_find_documents on wardsummaries: confirmed WardSummary documents with counts updated after demo (returned 3 summary docs with counts reflecting recent updates)

node src/ttl_check.js: set a bed's cleaningExpiresAt to now+5s and polled for 30s; TTL deletion was not observed within 30s (script logged repeated 'Still present'). This verifies TTL index exists but shows deletions may be delayed by server background sweep timing
not_verified: Precise TTL deletion timing: I attempted a short (5s) TTL expiry test and did not observe the document removed within 30s. TTL deletions are performed by a background sweeper and may run at intervals (commonly ~60s or more); I could not reliably observe the actual deletion timing within the short automated test. Recommendation: if your production logic depends on immediate deletion, rely on application-level checks or scheduled jobs; otherwise verify in your target environment how frequently the TTL background thread runs.

Any provisioning or resource creation of Azure DocumentDB clusters was intentionally not performed (run policy forbids Azure resource changes). The sample uses an existing cluster via DOCUMENTDB_URI (as provided in the run environment).
